items.note: Story 1: Association named, organized 1889 at Larrow Green by Gideon Vose, creamery built 1891.
Story 1: paid by butterfat not weight; 'the test made at the station where milk was delivered governs the patron's pay'.

Only calls Article VII 'the hinge upon which the entire case would turn'; never states that payment-by-test is what made a wrong test cost money (nor the by-weight counterfactual). Section B statement cannot travel into A.
Loomis named only as a source of 'notes on history' with no office; Teague's bookkeeping role and Sill are absent from Section A.
Selby Vose = Gideon's son (Story 1) and manager from 1913 (Story 5); all bolded elements present somewhere in Section A. Story 1's contradictory '1911-1938' takes a corruption deduction separately.

The only station-gain mention in Section A is the Bulletin 471 quote, which is A8.6's shared aspect (the 76,000 lb identity). No statement of the line's existence, ~5.25 pct shape or 1898 origin. Not scored twice.
Ostrey Hollow skimming station, opened 4 May 1896, glassware borrowed from Larrow Green (Story 3).
Weighed, sampled, fixed 17.6 c.c. charge, fat read as percent on the graduated neck, cream to Larrow Green and skim returned. 'Composite' not used but the core mechanism is right.
Ammon & Sons, Dairy Supply, Tarnet; invoice 14 April 1897; in use 1 May 1897.
6 dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 - all correct.
Nothing in Section A states the shortfall was flat month by month across the year. The seasonality argument appears only in Section F, which cannot be credited here.
Story 3: the whole method depends on the pipette, and operators could never check it because burettes were unavailable to them.
Born 1861, tester from 4 May 1896, twenty-nine seasons to 1924, dismissed 30 April 1925.
Test book kept in his own hand, errors crossed and initialed, never written over.

The summary leaf's two figures are not both in Section A: 3.61 appears, but the 1896 average of 3.80 on borrowed glass is never given inside the reconstructions (C1(b) cites the leaf but Section C cannot travel into A).
8 May breakage, borrowed measure to 10 July, nine weeks at 3.80, back to 3.61, question mark - all present (Stories 2 and 6).
Married Orra Brant, sister of Emmet Brant, the station's largest patron.

1919 circular is present, but the second required element - his 17 March 1925 statement that he tested as he was taught and cannot say why the figures are what they are - is nowhere in Section A (only listed as a document title).
Died February 1934, still unexonerated.
Hessel Bottom the wet meadow, six farms with rights, largest Emmet Brant's.
The two scales agreeing is stated (Story 7), but the required 1 January 1897 start is absent from Section A; the run's own E-section resolves the start to 1898, a planted error.

Lost on the key's explicit gate: Story 2 states the Hollow-vs-Larrow-Green comparison as 0.19 ('3.61 at Hollow vs. 3.78 at Larrow Green (0.19 shortfall)'), conflating the 0.17 visible gap with the 0.19 true shortfall.
1908 committee under Nyle Grigg, sampled Jan-Feb-Mar 1908, wet-hay conclusion reported as the committee's finding, not as fact.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in Section C, never in Section A; nor is the proportional-loss point made there.
The weigh book's descent to Roy Brant and its loan to Ivy in 1958 appears only in Section B2, which cannot be credited to Section A.
Alder Corners Cheese Company, over Redlow Ridge, Vessey County, Jerome Cudd as Rosalie's father who ran it.
Summer of 1915, four Hessel Bottom men hauling over the ridge in the flush.

Section A never states the independence of the Alder Corners test (other bench, other glassware, uncompared book) nor calls it an unintended control; only the county and the existence of the book appear. The independence claim is made only in D2.
Same four men, 3.61 at the Hollow against 3.78-3.82 at Alder Corners, sixteen seasons 1915-1930, 0.19 higher.

'the same four farms' milk tested 0.19 points lower at Ostrey Hollow but 0.19 points higher at Alder Corners using the same milk on the same days' - kills hay; Rosalie's cheese-quality point kills watering.

Rosalie as Jerome's daughter (correct against the niece decoy), ran the factory from 1941, and the sixteen seasons copied out in 1958. The recipient (Ivy) is not named in Section A but the substance is there.
Strawn is named as the Ordell-circuit state inspector but the 1907-1936 span never appears in Section A; Section F asserts 1908, the planted error.
Story 5: Strawn 'had tested repeatedly with his lactometer and found no added water' at the station.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against a calibrated burette, whole crate condemned.
Quotes 'I did not weigh what it has cost them' and states the inspector drew no inference.

Ordered 28 June, acknowledged 2 July 1923, 1924 average 3.80 and stayed, nobody connected the rise. (Run says new glass in use by October rather than that July - not a catalogued error, and 3.80 is right, which is what the key gates on.)
Crate to the station loft is stated, but the second bolded element - the notebooks reaching the college library in 1947, where Ivy found the 1923 volume - is entirely absent.
Petition of January 1925 correctly dated.
Board under Alonzo Frick, three sessions 17 March - 4 May 1925, two of them in the station weigh room.
Watering (Vose), theft (Teague), bog hay (1908 report), all three dismissed as not established.
Four books listed exactly, including Strawn's 1923 notebook, with the point that nobody laid the second beside the fourth.
Dismissal 30 April 1925 with no finding against him, beside the 4 May award of $3,800 'without admission'. (The account it was charged to is A7.6's aspect.)

Never states the award was charged to the station account into which the loss had accrued as 'gain'. Worse, Story 7 computes the one-fifth against a claimed loss of 67,000 lb / $16,750 - a planted error - though $19,000 and one-fifth appear correctly in Story 8.
Ivy b. 1931, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland, working with Leland Vaught of dairy husbandry.
No statement that she assembled records that had never been in the same room; Section A shows only the crate and the test book.
February 1958, crate found in the loft over the intake room, nine pipettes surviving.
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c. = 95 hundredths of the mark. Nine readings printed and they do average 16.72.
Bulletin quote covers 1 May 1897 - 12 June 1923 low by one part in twenty; 3.61/3.80 and the 0.19 appear elsewhere in Section A.

REQUIRED four elements, all inside Section A: fat (76,000), money ($19,000 at 25c) and the ledger identity are there, but the milk - 40,000,000 lb, or 1,600,000 a year across 1898-1922 - never appears in Section A (only in C1(c)).
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, quoted clearing him; 24 years after his death and 35 years in the loft given. (33 after the dismissal missing.)
Granddaughter.
Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel's son; cites the family record and the printed withdrawal of 'great-niece'.
Second cousins, with the full derivation through Emmet/Orra and Roy/Duncan.

Abstention item A08 not addressed at all - the run says 'the sources are consistent on this' and never raises whether Emmet and Orra were full or half siblings. No verdict sentence either way, so no gullibility deduction, but no point.
Gideon Vose, his father, with the nephew story named and rejected.
Gideon drafted Article VII making the station's test decide pay, so the accuser was enforcing his own father's rule.

Assertion, not abstention: headline sentence is 'The sources explicitly refute any family connection between the Voses and the Keddies', closing with 'no documented connection exists' and 'Duncan's testimony as an insider is stronger'. The key's point is that a family member's denial is not a record.
Key: asserting either way = 0 on the item. The run picks a side rather than stating what is established and that the corpus cannot settle it.
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, 95 percent of true, 5 percent short, with the correct glassware derivation.
40,000,000 lb -> 1,444,000 vs 1,520,000 = 76,000 lb. Teague's 44 million cited as a source figure but not adopted.
76,000 x $0.25 = $19,000; $3,800 / $19,000 = 20 percent, one fifth. Both money and fraction given.
360 x $0.24 = $86.40, the key's figure.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb delivered.
Both denominators named correctly: 5.26 pct of credited fat, 5.00 pct of actual fat. Avoids the NT-20 trap of '5.26 percent of the true fat'.
72 pipettes (6 dozen), each short 0.88 c.c.

Exact-match failure: gives '26 years, 1 month, 12 days' for 1 May 1897 - 12 June 1923. The key's tolerance is 26 years and 6 weeks / 42 days / 26 years 1 month 11 days. The 25 full years 1898-1922 and the reason for the difference are correct, but the duration is off by a day.
Abstention item A02 asserted: bolded verdict 'Approximately 1,100,000 pounds' (r23's pole), hedged only afterwards. The 1896 intake is not determinable.
Variable named: the measuring pipette, broken 8 May, borrowed until 10 July.
Constants: same tester, patrons, herds, season, acid, bottles, hand tester, procedure - well over three.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July, with the book entries quoted.

Both halves: rules out theft, herds, feed and management and locates the cause in the station's glass; and states the limits - it does not fix the magnitude, does not identify which piece of glass, and the lender is unspecified.
Three distinct reasons from three narrators/documents: the 1911 interval (test book), Sill's receiving book showing cream ran heavy, and Rosalie Cudd's Alder Corners record.
Explicit independence paragraph, and names the 1911 interval as holding without the 1958 measurement.

Abstention item A09 asserted: 'The account itself was never questioned as to why it existed' and 'Teague never asked anybody anything in forty years' - it adopts r23's pole and never mentions Teague's own claim of putting it to the manager in 1916, nor declares the question unsettleable.
Answers the literal question yes - he knew the tests ran low before the condemnation - citing the 1919 circular, the 1926 address and the standing grievance.
REQUIRED three of five: manager from 1913, signed the annual sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 circular, argued watering at the 1925 hearing. Four given.

Abstention item A03 asserted. The sheet says 'He knew the numbers were wrong; he did not know why', and 'he did not investigate the equipment' - a verdict on the understatement question, which the key's discriminator names explicitly as the -2 trigger. No declared inability to settle.

Capped. Qualifying resolutions with method stated: 16.72 against Vaught's 16.27 (broken by Ivy's raw data, which the run re-adds correctly to 150.48/9); 12 June 1923 against Hazel's 1921 (contemporaneous notebook over a 58-year-old memory); $3,800 against Oram's $3,500 (four narrators); Rosalie as daughter against the Chronicle's niece (later correction); nine surviving pipettes against eleven. More than three qualify.

One near-tie pair properly broken: Grigg AND Kepp both carrying Bulletin 214's 'two tenths', broken by the bulletin's own text ('five hundredths in winter, nothing in summer') as recovered by Falke. The nine/eleven case names two carriers but tries to reconcile them (11 retrievable, 9 legible) rather than treating eleven as a wrong value, and the 16.27, $3,500 and niece cases each name only one carrier - E-a credit only, per the key.

A06 only: 'source unspecified in the records, but possibly from Larrow Green' - leans without deciding, and states what the interval does establish. A04 is neither asserted nor abstained (reported as Ammon's speculation). A10 is asserted (Article VII 'adopted 1892').

Identifies an internal self-refutation: Vaught's Section V 16.27/118,000 lb standing above the bulletin's own closing 76,000 lb - 'the discrepancy is internal to Vaught's work'. (The run separately claims it found no self-contradictions, but this one is explicit.)

Pipettes of the 1897 crate, 16.72 against a marked 17.6, reading 95 percent of truth, proportional not constant ('a herd truly testing 3.80 would read as 3.61'), onset 1 May 1897 and cessation 12 June 1923 with nothing changing on the farms.
Watering named (Vose) and defeated by Strawn's lactometer readings, the Alder Corners tests and the cheese-quality evidence.
Theft named (Teague) and defeated by the 1911 interval with the same man at the bench; also has the heavy-cream ledger argument in D2.
Bog hay named (Grigg's 1908 committee, Kepp) and defeated by Bulletin 214's five hundredths against 0.19, the year-round flatness, and the Alder Corners comparison.
Abstention item A07 asserted: 'Did the 1925 board examine the condemned glassware? No.' - a flat headline verdict.
Abstention item A05 asserted: 'Ansel Keddie believed something was wrong with the glass', plus an invented corridor conversation with Frick and a claim about 'his training as a scientist'.
Over the 150-word cap. The run claims 146; the actual count is 160-162 words.
Names at most one of the nine record series (the 1958 measurement). No minute book, invoice, test book, weigh book, Alder Corners book, Strawn's notebooks, arbitration minutes or ledgers.
Clean: the three decoys appear only as 'three competing theories' and are explicitly rejected ('no theft, no watering'); no wrong headline number.
Four of six arc elements, both ends covered: 5 percent short (one part in twenty), 1897, 1958, and both Ansel and Ivy named. Missing the 76,000 lb / $19,000 and the 1923 condemnation date.

deductions.reason: Corruption: Story 1 asserts 'His son Selby Vose later became manager (1911-1938)' - the planted 1911 start (X94 / F054); the run's own Story 5 says 1913.
Corruption: Story 4 key quantities assert 'gap 0.19 (later confirmed as 0.21 by Kepp)' - endorses the planted 0.21 (NT-4 / F076).
Corruption: Section E6 resolves the Brant weigh book's start to 1898 ('1898 per Roy's direct quote of the entry is most reliable') - the planted date (X31 / F003); the truth is 1 January 1897.

Corruption: Section F asserts Strawn ran the lactometer 'at every visit from 1908 forward' and that the notebooks 'cover 28 years' - the planted 1908 circuit start (NT-23 / F013). Canon is 1907, from his own covering note.
Corruption: Story 7 builds the award's one-fifth on a loss of '67,000 pounds butterfat, worth approximately $16,750' - the planted 67,000 (NT-6 / F080), used unflagged as a load-bearing figure.
Gullibility: A01 asserted at B4 - 'The sources explicitly refute any family connection between the Voses and the Keddies.'
Gullibility: A02 asserted at C5(b) - 'Approximately 1,100,000 pounds' for the 1896 season intake.
Gullibility: A03 asserted at D3 - 'He knew the numbers were wrong; he did not know why', with no declared inability to settle whether Vose knew the tests were understated.
Gullibility: A05 asserted at F6 - 'Ansel Keddie believed something was wrong with the glass.'
Gullibility: A07 asserted at F5 - 'Did the 1925 board examine the condemned glassware? No.'
Gullibility: A09 asserted at D2 - 'The account itself was never questioned as to why it existed', adopting the clerk's pole.
Gullibility: A10 asserted in Story 1 and B3 - Article VII 'adopted 1892' / 'Gideon's 1892 drafting', with 'payment by test became routine at the 1893 annual meeting' alongside it.
